source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's HOU3-HOU4 campus in Houston publishes 84 MW of IT capacity across 347,000 square feet of technical space, the largest published figure of any facility mapped in Texas.

That is the only number here that speaks to AI scale. The density implied by those two figures is about 242 square feet per megawatt, which is a floorplan fact, not a compute fact, and it says nothing about what silicon goes inside. To turn 84 MW into racks you have to assume a rack density, and the operator does not publish one. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 84 MW of IT load is roughly 2,100 racks. At 10 kW per rack, a more traditional enterprise density, the same load is roughly 8,400 racks. The gap between those two numbers is the whole story of whether this campus matters to AI, and it is not resolvable from the spec page.

The single certification listed, Green Globes, is a whole-building environmental rating, and it qualifies the campus for general commercial occupancy rather than for any specific tenant or workload. No tenant, no accelerator count, no power procurement, and no interconnection status is published.

Texas is the deepest market mapped, with 137 facilities, but only 19 of them publish a megawatt figure at all. Those 19 total 475.41 MW, which means this one campus is 17.7 percent of all published Texas capacity. That share is a statement about disclosure as much as about construction. Most of the state's mapped footprint is invisible in capacity terms, so a single operator willing to publish a number can top a ranking without that ranking meaning what it appears to mean.
